 Tue, November 10, 2026 at 11:06 AM Shae’s CRPS journey: How DRG therapy helped her return to an active life Comment on this story 0 Comment Share story Share After a cheerleading stunt led to major leg surgeries, Shae Eichele-Gawry faced years of severe pain before receiving a Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS) diagnosis. She and Dr. Allen Burton joined We Are Austin to talk about CRPS symptoms and Shae’s experience with DRG therapy. 
 Watch the full conversation above to hear Shae’s story and learn more about CRPS.
 Years of pain after an injury
 CRPS can cause severe, ongoing pain that lasts beyond the expected healing period after an injury or surgery. Dr. Burton said symptoms may include burning pain, skin discoloration, swelling, tingling, and other unusual sensations near the affected area. He said the condition affects about 200,000 Americans every year.
 Shae was 18 when she was dropped during a cheerleading stunt in 2018. After two major reconstructions of her left leg, she went through physical therapy and followed a typical orthopedic recovery plan. But her pain kept getting worse.
 “It felt like someone had a match and put it under my leg and lit it with gasoline,” Shae said.
 She was diagnosed with CRPS in 2020. Dr. Burton said patients may first be evaluated by a surgeon or primary care physician and then referred to a pain specialist.
 Finding a treatment that helped
 After her diagnosis, Shae tried medication and injections before receiving a dorsal root ganglion (DRG) stimulator. Dr. Burton described the Abbott Proclaim DRG system as a small wire placed near the DRG that delivers a gentle electrical pulse to quiet irritated nerves.
 He said his team generally sees a response in more than 80% of patients during both the trial and subsequent implant. Shae said her own pain has decreased by 80%.
 “DRG gave me a second chance,” she said.
 Today, Shae is back to an active lifestyle and is a champion bodybuilder. She said the treatment helped her return to the life she loves.
 For more information about CRPS and DRG therapy, visit AboutYourPain.com.
